title: 1 Kings 6:1–13
context: 1 Kings 6:1–13 dates the beginning of the temple’s construction to the four hundred eightieth year after the exodus and the fourth year of Solomon, and gives the main dimensions of the house, its porch, windows, and side chambers. Stones are prepared at the quarry so no iron tool is heard at the site. Interpreters use the 480-year figure in different ways when dating the exodus, and readers in both traditions hold differing views on that chronology. In the middle of the building account the LORD’s word comes to Solomon: if he walks in God’s statutes, God will establish his word to David, dwell among Israel, and not forsake his people. Both traditions treat this word as shared ground: the house matters because of God’s covenant presence, and obedience matters more than the building itself.

verses.text: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon begins to build the LORD’s house in the 480th year after the exodus, in the fourth year of his reign, in the month Ziv. Arminian readers see the exodus as the reference point, linking the temple with God’s deliverance of Israel. They also note that interpreters differ on how to use the number for dating the exodus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the exodus framing is theologically significant. Some take the 480 years as a literal chronology and others as a schematic figure, and both views are found in each tradition. Both traditions agree the temple marks a new stage in God’s dwelling with Israel.

verses.text: The house which King Solomon built for the LORD had a length of sixty cubits, and its width twenty, and its height thirty cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: The house is sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high. Arminians read the measurements as a practical record of the building, and they see a carefully planned house built to honor the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the main dimensions are often observed to be double those of the tabernacle’s tent. Both traditions read the measurements, with a cubit often estimated at about 18 inches, as description rather than as a point of theological difference.

verses.text: The porch in front of the temple of the house had a length of twenty cubits, which was along the width of the house. Ten cubits was its width in front of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The porch in front of the house is twenty cubits wide along the house’s width and ten cubits deep. Arminian readers see the porch as the entrance to the temple, through which worshipers approached the house of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the layout moving from the porch to the main hall to the inner sanctuary, a pattern of increasing holiness. Both traditions read the verse as part of the description and avoid building theology on the dimensions.

verses.text: He made windows of fixed lattice work for the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes windows of fixed lattice work for the house. Arminians read the detail as part of the building account, and they note that the precise meaning of the Hebrew description of the windows is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the architectural term is difficult and has been translated in different ways. Both traditions treat the verse as construction detail rather than as symbolism, without speculating beyond what the text describes.

verses.text: Against the wall of the house, he built floors all around, against the walls of the house all around, both of the temple and of the inner sanctuary; and he made side rooms all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds floors and side rooms around the walls of the temple and inner sanctuary. Arminian readers see the side rooms as practical storage and work spaces for the temple’s service, part of a well-planned building.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that such side rooms may have stored temple supplies and treasures. Both traditions read the verse as building detail and avoid speculating beyond what the text says about their purpose.

verses.text: The lowest floor was five cubits wide, and the middle was six cubits wide, and the third was seven cubits wide; for on the outside he made offsets in the wall of the house all around, that the beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The side floors are five, six, and seven cubits wide, with offsets in the wall so the beams did not have to be inserted into the walls of the house. Arminians see careful engineering that kept the main walls intact, showing the skill put into the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the stepped walls that allowed each floor to rest on a ledge. Both traditions read the verse as technical description that honors careful workmanship, without turning it into a theological contrast.

verses.text: The house, when it was under construction, was built of stone prepared at the quarry; and no hammer or ax or any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was under construction.
verses.arminianNotes: The house is built with stone prepared at the quarry, so no hammer, ax, or iron tool is heard at the site. Arminian readers see reverence in the quiet construction, and many recall the law against using tools on altar stones (Exodus 20:25), though the connection is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the narrator presents the silence as remarkable. Some interpreters draw a devotional application about God building his people quietly, and both traditions offer that only as an application, not as the verse’s direct meaning.

verses.text: The door for the middle side rooms was in the right side of the house. They went up by winding stairs into the middle floor, and out of the middle into the third.
verses.arminianNotes: The door to the middle side rooms is on the right side of the house, with winding stairs up to the middle and third floors. Arminians read the detail as part of the practical layout, showing that the building was designed for ongoing use.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The word translated "winding stairs" is uncertain and may refer to a different kind of passage. Both traditions treat the verse as construction detail and avoid building theology on it.

verses.text: So he built the house and finished it; and he covered the house with beams and planks of cedar.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds and finishes the house and covers it with cedar beams and planks. Arminian readers see the completion of the main structure as Solomon faithfully carrying out the work God had promised his father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the narrative returns to the completion of the house in 6:14 and 6:38. Both traditions read the verse as part of the building account, with the cedar showing the quality of materials used.

verses.text: He built the floors all along the house, each five cubits high; and they rested on the house with timbers of cedar.
verses.arminianNotes: He builds the side floors along the house, each five cubits high, resting on the house with cedar timbers. Arminians read the verse as completing the description of the side rooms, part of a careful and orderly construction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and treat the verse as technical description. Both traditions note that the account is interrupted immediately afterward by the LORD’s word in 6:11–13, which shifts the focus from the building to the covenant.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Solomon, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Solomon. Arminian readers see God speaking in the middle of the building project, showing that his concern is not only with stones and cedar but with the faithfulness of the king and people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the placement of this word as significant: the building account is interrupted to remind Solomon what really matters. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a covenant word that is shared ground between them.

verses.text: “Concerning this house which you are building, if you will walk in my statutes, and execute my ordinances, and keep all my commandments to walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father.
verses.arminianNotes: God says that if Solomon walks in his statutes, ordinances, and commandments, he will establish his word to David. Arminians see a real condition calling Solomon to faithful obedience, and they read Solomon’s later failures (1 Kings 11) in light of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that obedience is required and that the warning is real. Both traditions note that God’s promise to David’s line continues through grace even when kings fail (2 Samuel 7:14–16), and they treat the verse as shared ground on the importance of obedience.

verses.text: I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: God promises to dwell among Israel and not forsake his people. Arminian readers see God’s presence as the real purpose of the temple, a gift that calls for faithful response from the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the promise as part of God’s covenant commitment, later fulfilled in Christ dwelling among his people (John 1:14). Both traditions agree that God’s presence, not the building itself, is what makes the temple significant.
